relevance_reason: The paper first describes NIT1-related small vessel disease (BSVD4): 7 patients from 5 pedigrees with bi-allelic NIT1 variants, plus functional evidence.

findings.statement: Rutten et al. (2024) described NIT1-small vessel disease as a new autosomal recessive cerebral small vessel disease. It is caused by loss-of-function variants in NIT1 and is characterized by a triad of movement disorders, massively dilated perivascular spaces in the basal ganglia, and intracerebral hemorrhage.
quotes: NIT1-small vessel disease is a novel, autosomal recessively inherited cerebral small vessel disease characterized by a triad of movement disorders, massively dilated basal ganglia perivascular spaces, and intracerebral hemorrhage.

phenotypes.text: massively dilated basal ganglia perivascular spaces

findings.statement: Rutten et al. (2024) reported 7 patients with NIT1-small vessel disease from 5 unrelated pedigrees: 3 siblings and 4 single cases. The patients presented in mid-adulthood with movement disorders. All had striking abnormalities on brain MRI, with numerous and massively dilated perivascular spaces in the basal ganglia. Three patients had a non-lobar intracerebral hemorrhage between ages 45 and 60, which was fatal in 2 of them.
quotes: Patients presented in mid-adulthood with movement disorders. All patients had striking abnormalities on brain magnetic resonance imaging, with numerous and massively dilated basal ganglia perivascular spaces.
Three patients had non-lobar intracerebral hemorrhage between age 45 and 60, which was fatal in 2 cases.

phenotypes.text: numerous massively dilated basal ganglia perivascular spaces

findings.statement: Rutten et al. (2024) found on brain autopsy large electron-dense deposits in the walls of small and medium-sized cerebral arteries.
quotes: Brain autopsy revealed large electron-dense deposits in the vessel walls of small and medium sized cerebral arteries.

phenotypes.text: electron-dense deposits in cerebral arterial walls

findings.statement: Rutten et al. (2024) used exome sequencing in 3 sibs with NIT1-small vessel disease. All 3 were compound heterozygous for 2 NIT1 variants: c.727C>T (p.Arg243Trp) and c.198_199del (p.Ala68Ter).
quotes: The first identified patients were 3 siblings, compound heterozygous for the NIT1 c.727C>T; (p.Arg243Trp) variant and the NIT1 c.198_199del; p.(Ala68∗) variant.

findings.statement: Rutten et al. (2024) reported 4 more patients with NIT1-small vessel disease, each a single case from 1 of 4 unrelated pedigrees. All 4 were homozygous for the NIT1 c.727C>T (p.Arg243Trp) variant.
quotes: The 4 additional patients were single cases from 4 unrelated pedigrees and were all homozygous for the NIT1 c.727C>T; p.(Arg243Trp) variant.

findings.statement: Rutten et al. (2024) found by Western blotting that NIT1 protein was absent from patient fibroblasts. Metabolic analysis of patient urine confirmed loss of NIT1 enzyme function.
quotes: Western blotting on patient fibroblasts showed absence of NIT1 protein, and metabolic analysis in urine confirmed loss of NIT1 enzymatic function.

relevance_reason: Reports a family with basal ganglia cavitating lesions and compound heterozygous NIT1 loss-of-function variants, with biochemical and functional evidence. This is the founding description of the disorder.

findings.statement: Rendu et al. (2019) described 3 brothers with bilateral small cystic lesions of the basal ganglia (a deep cavitating state) and positive urine sulfite dipstick tests. The index patient (II.4) had nonsevere mental retardation and an acute psychotic episode followed by generalized seizures. At age 34 he developed a sudden pure motor left hemiparesis. Arteriography, EEG, EMG, Doppler ultrasound and echocardiography were normal. Over 20 years he progressed to severe neuropsychological deterioration and spastic tetraplegia, and he died at age 57.
quotes: He had a history of a nonsevere mental retardation, and was admitted 2 years before in psychiatry unit for an acute psychotic episode followed by generalized seizures.
A computed tomography scan (CT scan) and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) T1 and T2 (0.5 T) showed bilateral small cystic lesions affecting basal ganglia.
The clinical status of the patient progressively worsened over a 20 years period with a severe neuropsychological deterioration and a spastic tetraplegia.

findings.statement: Rendu et al. (2019) reported that a brother of the index patient (II.5) had diabetes mellitus and had led an active professional life. At age 58 he had a sudden coma with cardiovascular collapse. CT and 3T MRI showed the same basal ganglia cystic lesions, and his urine sulfite test was positive. He recovered but had neuropsychological deterioration (BREF 14/18, MMSE 22/30). A third brother (II.7), diagnosed with schizophrenia 40 years earlier, had a normal clinical examination but the same brain lesions and a positive urine sulfite test.
quotes: He was a 58 years old man with a history of diabetes mellitus and had lived an active professional life.
The patient progressively recovered but presented with a neuropsychological deterioration (BREF: 14/18, MMSE: 22/30).

A third brother of the family was in a psychiatric institution for a schizophrenia diagnosed 40 years ago (II.7). His clinical examination was normal, but the CT scan and the MRI (3 T) found the same brain lesions together with a positive urine sulfite test.

findings.statement: In 2 affected brothers (II.5 and II.7), Rendu et al. (2019) used exome sequencing to identify compound heterozygous variants in the NIT1 gene. One was a c.457G>A transition (p.Gly153Arg) at a highly conserved residue on the last nucleotide of exon 4. Sequencing of the NIT1 transcript from a skin biopsy of patient II.5 showed that this variant affected splicing. Asymptomatic sibs whose DNA was available carried neither variant. Cloning showed that the 2 variants were on different alleles. NIT1 protein was undetectable on western blot of the patient's fibroblasts.
quotes: two rare variants were found in the NIT1 gene (Nitrilase‐like protein 1, NM_005600): an heterozygous c.457G > A;p.Gly153Arg variation and an heterozygous c.670dupA;p.Thr224Asnfs*41 variation

It is also located on the last nucleotide of exon 4 and predicted to affect the splicing of NIT1 mRNA, which was next demonstrated by sequencing of the NIT1 transcript extracted from a skin biopsy of patient II.5 (data not shown).
Accordingly, the level of Nit1 protein was undetectable by western blot in fibroblasts from patient II.5 (Fig. 1D).

findings.statement: Rendu et al. (2019) found that the second NIT1 variant in the affected brothers was a 1-bp duplication, c.670dupA, causing a frameshift (p.Thr224Asnfs*41) that was predicted to cause loss of function. It was inherited from the asymptomatic mother. The father's DNA was not available.
quotes: The c.670dupA variant is predicted to induce a loss of function of the NIT1 allele due to a frameshift in the coding sequence.
The familial study showed that asymptomatic brothers and sisters, whose DNA was available, had neither of the variants, and that the c.670dupA was inherited from the asymptomatic mother.

findings.statement: Rendu et al. (2019) found that the affected brothers had positive urine sulfite dipstick tests, whereas the mother and the asymptomatic sibs who were tested did not. GC/MS organic acid analysis detected a urinary compound with a mass spectrum identical to deaminated glutathione (dGSH), matching the compound excreted by Nit1-knockout mice. It was present in the 3 affected brothers but undetectable in the other sibs tested and the mother. The authors proposed that dGSH accumulation was probably responsible for the positive sulfite test.
quotes: A qualitative organic acid analysis profile10 on urine samples of members of the family identified in individuals mutated for NIT1 an unusual compound with a mass spectrum identical to dGSH (Fig. 1E).
The same peaks were observed in urine of his brothers (II.5 and II.7) but were undetectable in the other siblings tested and the mother.
The loss of function of the gene led to the accumulation of dGSH, which was detected in the urine of patients, and probably responsible for the positive urine sulfite test.

findings.statement: In fibroblasts from patient II.5, Rendu et al. (2019) found unchanged cytoplasmic Cu/Zn SOD activity but a 2-fold increase in mitochondrial MnSOD activity. They suggested that dGSH accumulation causes oxidative stress and redox damage. They also noted that other effects of NIT1 deficiency, such as altered Wnt/beta-catenin signaling, could contribute.
quotes: The cytoplasmic SOD (Cu/Zn SOD) activity was not changed, whilst the activity of the mitochondrial SOD (MnSOD) showed a twofold increase as compared to control samples
dGSH may represent a toxic metabolite, whose accumulation would interfere with the glutathione metabolism and in the long term possibly induce redox damages.

findings.statement: Rendu et al. (2019) concluded that this is a novel autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by NIT1 mutations. It combines neurological signs, basal ganglia lesions and a positive urine sulfite test. The authors excluded sulfite oxidase deficiency and molybdenum cofactor deficiency.
quotes: Overall, we described here a novel autosomal recessive metabolic disorder due to mutations in the NIT1 gene which associates neurological signs, basal ganglia lesions as well as positive urine sulfite test
These pathologies were excluded and we identify here a novel nosological entity.

findings.statement: Rendu et al. (2019) suggested that the urine sulfite test could easily be used to screen cohorts of psychiatric patients for the disorder.
quotes: positive urine sulfite test, the latter being easily used to screen for the disease in cohorts of psychiatric patients
